explain.what: Whether the share price is above or below its average price over the last ~10 months.
explain.why: Big funds buy and sell around this line, so being above it usually means buyers are in control. It is slow: it confirms a turn after it has happened.
explain.score: The price is above its long-run average: the long-term trend is up.

explain.what: Whether the shorter trend (last ~10 weeks) is running above or below the longer trend (last ~10 months).
explain.why: It shows whether the trend itself is turning, not just where the price is today.
explain.score: The shorter trend is above the longer one: momentum is building upward.

indicators.name: Relative strength vs peers, 3 months
indicators.measured: equal-weighted average of 6 peers over 63 trading days

explain.what: Whether the stock has done better or worse than its direct competitors over the last 3 months.
explain.why: It separates something specific to this company from a whole-industry move.
explain.score: Lagging its competitors: the market is favouring rivals right now.

indicators.name: Buying vs selling volume
indicators.measured: volume on up days ÷ down days, last 20 trading days

explain.what: Whether more shares change hands on days the price rises than on days it falls (last 20 trading days).
explain.why: Large investors leave footprints in trading volume; heavy buying days suggest they are accumulating.
explain.score: Trading is balanced between up and down days.

indicators.name: Short interest trend
indicators.note: Neutral: only 0.9% of freely traded shares are sold short, below the 2% minimum for a move to count.

explain.what: How many shares are borrowed and sold by investors betting the price will fall, and whether that is growing.
explain.why: Short sellers often do deep research, so a rising number of bets against a stock is a warning worth noticing.
explain.score: Bets against the stock are steady.

indicators.name: Institutional ownership change
indicators.measured: shares added minus shares cut by institutions last quarter, as % of shares outstanding
indicators.note: Proxy: counts changes in existing positions, not new or closed ones.

explain.what: Whether professional investment firms, in total, added or cut shares last quarter.
explain.why: Shows whether the big money is moving in or out. It arrives late (filings come up to 45 days after the quarter).
explain.score: Funds were broadly steady last quarter.

indicators.name: Dollar backdrop (shared macro)
indicators.measured: the dollar index 20 trading days earlier

explain.what: Whether the US dollar has strengthened or weakened over the last month.
explain.why: A strong dollar pulls money out of riskier assets worldwide and shrinks the dollar value of overseas sales.
explain.score: The dollar has strengthened: a headwind for stocks.

indicators.name: Fed rate expectations (shared macro)
indicators.measured: net odds (cut minus rise) for the next Fed meeting, 28 days earlier
indicators.note: Now: 1% cut, 24% rise; a month ago: 5% cut, 27% rise.

explain.what: Whether markets now expect the Fed to cut or raise interest rates at its next meeting, compared with a month ago.
explain.why: Interest rates set the price of every other asset; expectations move long before the Fed acts.

indicators.name: Revenue growth trend
indicators.measured: average growth of the prior 4 quarters, each vs a year earlier

explain.what: Whether sales growth is speeding up or slowing down compared with the past year.
explain.why: The plainest evidence of whether customers want more of what the company sells.

indicators.name: Gross margin trend (one-offs removed)
indicators.measured: gross margin of the 4 quarters a year earlier
indicators.note: Adjusted for one-offs: tariff refunds (one-time benefit, about 2 points of margin) (−$2,200m to gross profit, quarter to 2026-06-27; Apple Q3 FY26 results call, via beancount.io 22 Aug 2026). As reported: 48.7% vs 46.7% (+2.0 pts).

explain.what: Whether the share of each sales dollar kept as gross profit is rising or falling.
explain.why: A company that can hold or raise its margins has pricing power, a sign of strong demand.
explain.score: Margins are rising: the company is holding its prices well.

indicators.name: Earnings forecast revisions
indicators.measured: consensus EPS for the year to 2027-09-30, 90 days earlier

explain.what: Whether analysts have raised or cut their profit forecasts over the last 3 months.
explain.why: Changes in expected profit are one of the most reliable drivers of share prices over the following months.

indicators.name: Guidance vs expectations
indicators.measured: analysts' consensus revenue growth for the September quarter when guidance was given (30 Jul 2026)
indicators.source: Apple Q3 FY26 call; consensus per Investing.com
indicators.note: Apple guided 9-11% revenue growth vs about 12% expected. Apple only guides one quarter ahead, so DM3 scores guidance vs expectations (Kenneth's decision, 30 Sep 2026).

explain.what: Whether management's outlook for next quarter came in above or below what analysts expected.
explain.why: Management knows its order book best; its outlook is an early read on demand.
explain.score: Management guided below expectations: demand or costs look worse than the market thought.

indicators.name: Services revenue growth
indicators.source: Apple quarterly results release, net sales by category (on results)

explain.what: Growth in Apple's Services revenue (App Store, iCloud, Apple Music, payments) vs the same quarter last year.
explain.why: Services is recurring and far more profitable than hardware, so it drives much of Apple's profit growth and its valuation.
explain.score: Services is growing fast: the high-margin engine is healthy.

indicators.name: iPhone revenue growth
indicators.source: Apple quarterly results release, net sales by category (on results)

explain.what: Growth in iPhone revenue vs the same quarter last year.
explain.why: iPhone is about half of Apple's revenue and brings customers into the Services ecosystem.

indicators.name: Apple smartphone shipments (research firms)
indicators.measured: same calendar quarter a year earlier
indicators.source: Counterpoint / IDC / Canalys quarterly press releases

explain.what: How many iPhones were shipped in the latest calendar quarter vs the same quarter a year earlier, from an independent research firm (IDC; firms can disagree, see Known defects).
explain.why: It arrives before Apple reports, so it is an early outside read on demand.
explain.score: Shipments are growing: demand is holding up.

indicators.name: Forward P/E vs peers
indicators.measured: median of the peer set (next 12 months, same rule)
indicators.note: Next 12 months: blends consensus EPS for the years to 2026-09-30 and 2027-09-30 ($9.58). Yahoo's next-fiscal-year figure: 34.5x.

explain.what: How much investors pay for each dollar of the company's expected profit, compared with its competitors.
explain.why: Paying much more than for rivals means good news is already in the price, so there is less room for disappointment.
explain.score: Much more expensive than its competitors: the price assumes things keep going very well.

explain.what: The same comparison as above, but allowing for how fast profits are expected to grow.
explain.why: A higher price can be fair if profits grow faster; this checks whether they do.
explain.score: Still expensive after allowing for its expected growth.

indicators.name: EV/EBITDA vs peers
indicators.note: EV = market value + debt − cash ($4,843bn) ÷ last-12-month EBITDA ($168.0bn).

explain.what: The company's total value (including debt) compared with its operating profit, against competitors.
explain.why: Unlike the P/E, this counts debt, so an indebted company cannot look artificially cheap.
explain.score: More expensive than its competitors once debt is counted.

indicators.name: P/E vs own 5-year history
indicators.measured: the stock's own median trailing P/E, last 5 years (weekly)
indicators.note: Trailing (last 12 months actual) P/E: free forward P/E history is too short.

explain.what: How much investors pay for each dollar of profit today, compared with this company's own usual level over 5 years.
explain.why: Shows whether the stock is cheap or expensive by its own standards, which catches whole-industry re-pricing.

Short interest rose 10.7% vs the previous month's report, but at only 0.9% of freely traded shares it is too small to count (the minimum is 2%).

This is day 3 of the 10 trading days of score history needed to confirm a call; next big test: results expected on 29 Oct.

Newer signals are softer than the scores. segments.name: iPhone
segments.buyers: Consumers and businesses worldwide, through Apple stores, phone carriers and resellers.
pos: Biggest and currently fastest-growing part: +19% over the last 4 quarters vs the 4 quarters before.
Every iPhone sold keeps or adds a user for Services (App Store, iCloud, Apple Music), which earns about 76% gross margin.
neg: Not recurring: sold once, and demand rises and falls with upgrade cycles.
Lower margin: Products earn about 39% gross margin (last 4 quarters), roughly half of Services' 76%.
Over half of Apple's sales depend on this one product.
Exposed to China demand, tariffs and component costs such as memory.

segments.name: Mac
segments.sells: Mac laptops and desktops, running Apple's own M-series chips.
segments.buyers: Consumers, students, creative professionals and businesses.
pos: Growing +10% (last 4 quarters vs the 4 before), and +29% in the June quarter vs a year earlier.
Keeps professionals inside Apple's ecosystem, which supports Services.
neg: One-off purchases, replaced every several years.
Products gross margin (about 39%), well below Services.

segments.name: iPad
pos: Strong in education and creative work; another entry point into Services.
neg: Barely growing: +2% (last 4 quarters vs the 4 before).
Share of sales down from 7.6% to 6.1% in 3 years.
Long replacement cycles.

segments.name: Wearables, Home & Accessories
segments.sells: Apple Watch, AirPods, Apple TV, HomePod, Vision Pro and accessories.
pos: Deepens the tie to iPhone (health, fitness, audio), which makes customers less likely to switch.
neg: Shrinking share: 10.5% to 7.8% of sales in 3 years; growth only +2% (last 4 quarters vs the 4 before), though +6% in the June quarter vs a year earlier.
Discretionary gadgets: first to be cut when consumers spend less.

segments.name: Services
segments.sells: App Store commissions, iCloud, Apple Music and TV+, AppleCare, Apple Pay, advertising, and licensing (including Google's payment to be the default search engine).
segments.buyers: People using Apple's installed base of more than 2.5 billion active devices (Apple, Jul 2026 call).
pos: Highest margin: about 76% gross margin (last 4 quarters) vs about 39% for products.
Mostly recurring: subscriptions and repeat spending, which smooths results between iPhone cycles.
Steady growth: +14% (last 4 quarters vs the 4 before) with little extra capital, so most of it turns into free cash flow.
neg: Regulators are pushing down App Store fees (EU Digital Markets Act; US court orders on outside payment links).
The Google search payment is under antitrust scrutiny; losing it would hit this high-margin income directly.
Share of sales flat this year (25.8% both years) because iPhone grew faster.

pos: The shift in mix alone added 1.5 pts to gross margin vs 3 years earlier (last 4 quarters vs the 4 quarters 3 years earlier, each part's margin held at that earlier level).
neg: Fastest-growing part (iPhone, +19% vs a year earlier) earns below the company gross margin.
Concentration: iPhone is 53% of sales (last 4 quarters).

shift.title: What the shift means for Apple
pos: Services rose from 21% to 26% of sales in 3 years (last 4 quarters vs the 4 quarters to Jun 2023). Company gross margin rose from 43.4% to 48.7% over the same period. About 1.5 points of that came from the shift towards Services; the rest came from higher margins within both Products (36.0% to 39.1%) and Services (70.7% to 76.0%).
More recurring revenue: about a quarter of sales now comes from subscriptions and repeat spending, which steadies profit and supports free cash flow between iPhone cycles.
Free cash flow (operating cash minus capital spending) was 29% of revenue over the last 4 quarters ($136.7bn), vs 24% for the 4 quarters a year earlier.
neg: Near term, memory costs are squeezing the Products margin: Apple guided September-quarter gross margin to 47-48%, below the 48.7% of the last 4 quarters, and that guide includes about 1 point of one-off tariff refunds.
This year the mix stood still: iPhone grew faster (+19%) than Services (+14%), so Services stayed at 26% of sales.
Over half of sales still depend on iPhone upgrade cycles.
Part of the high-margin Services income (App Store fees, the Google search payment) is under regulatory and legal pressure.

mix.note: Apple reports gross margin for Products and Services only, not for each product. So iPhone, Mac, iPad and Wearables all show the Products gross margin.

2026-09-30.lead: Apple is Building history (today's zone: Hold), at +5 on a −100 to +100 scale, up from +3 yesterday: a strong business priced for perfection, with interest-rate and dollar pressure still weighing on it.
bullets: The business is strong, with soft spots. Demand scores +43: revenue grew 16.4% in the June quarter vs a year earlier, faster than the 12.5% average of the prior four quarters; gross margin over the last 4 quarters was 48.2% vs 46.7% for the 4 quarters a year earlier once one-off tariff refunds are removed (48.7% as reported); Services revenue +12.1% and iPhone revenue +21.7% (June quarter vs a year earlier); IDC counts iPhone shipments +15% in Apr-Jun vs a year earlier. Soft spots: September-quarter guidance of 9-11% growth was below the ~12% analysts expected, gross margin is guided down to 47-48% (from 50.1% in the June quarter, which included about 2 points of one-off tariff refunds), and analysts' profit forecast for the year to Sep 2027 slipped 1.1% in 90 days.

It is priced for perfection. Valuation scores −76: investors pay 67% more per dollar of expected profit over the next 12 months than for the peer median (34.8x vs 20.8x forward P/E), 25% more after allowing for growth, and 44% more on EV/EBITDA (29.1x vs 20.3x). On trailing (last-12-month) earnings it is 22% above its own 5-year median (38.2x vs 31.3x); that scores as expensive only at +25%.

The money backdrop has turned. Liquidity scores −13, up from −27 yesterday: markets price a 34% chance of a Fed rate rise on 28 Oct, up from 27% a month earlier (Polymarket), and the dollar index is 1.80 points higher than 20 trading days earlier. Buying and selling volume is balanced (1.01x up-day vs down-day volume, last 20 trading days). Short interest rose 10.7% vs the previous month's report, but at only 0.9% of freely traded shares it is too small to count (the minimum is 2%).

The price trend is up but lagging, and the call is not yet confirmed. Price scores +44: Apple is 15.4% above its 200-day average, but 6.8 points behind its peers' average return over the last 3 months. It closed at $333.02, +1.1% on the day vs −0.25% for the S&P 500. This is day 2 of the 10 trading days of score history needed to confirm a call; next big test: results expected on 29 Oct.

Newer signals are softer than the scores. The Demand readings use April-June data. iPhone 18 Pro delivery waits in launch week were 7 days vs 15 for iPhone 17 Pro a year earlier, with the biggest drop in China (JPMorgan, 14 Sep); UBS (24 Sep) found waits about flat vs a year earlier outside China and 4 days shorter in China. Shorter waits can mean weaker demand or better supply: which one is not yet clear. Jefferies (Underperform, $263.66 target, 20% below the 29 Sep close) and Phillip Securities (Reduce, $290, 12% below) cut Apple on 11 Aug, citing memory costs and no clear sign that Apple Intelligence drives upgrades.

move.headline: A normal-sized pullback, mostly specific to Apple

evidence.t: Apple fell 2.2% while the S&P 500 slipped 0.3%. That is inside Apple's normal daily range, so no classification is triggered.
A secondary site linked the fall to a Bank of America note warning that AI shopping agents could divert App Store and payments revenue. Not confirmed by a primary source.

Shares closed 3.0% below their highest close of the past year ($341.10 on 25 Sep) ahead of the expected 29 Oct results, with the weaker September-quarter outlook (9-11% growth vs 16% in the June quarter, each vs a year earlier) still weighing.
Reported by one outlet, not confirmed by Apple: Apple has accepted a 2027 memory deal at about $2.00 per gigabit vs $1.50 now (+33%), with more product price rises likely.
